brief.outcome: Keep the cash balance at or above $150,000 in every week of the next six months, without losing either of the two biggest retail customers.

ambition.goal_beyond: The business pays for its own stock and growth from the profit it already makes, instead of living on the overdraft.
rungs: Build a cash forecast from the ledger and bank and show the first week the balance falls below $150,000
Find which levers (collecting faster, holding less timber, timing supplier payments) free the most cash, and choose a package that holds $150,000 for six months in a bad case too
Keep it true: a weekly roll-forward compares the forecast with the bank balance, so a slide towards the floor is flagged weeks before it costs an overdraft
ambition.judge: The bank statements: the actual weekly closing balance, compared with the forecast and with the $150,000 floor

brief.deliverable: A cash forecast in a Google Sheet that is rolled forward weekly, a chosen package of cash actions with drafts ready for the owner to use, and the first weekly check against the bank

answers.question: What business, and how big?
answers.answer: Furniture maker selling to retailers, revenue about $4.2M a year, 12% net margin (last year's accounts)

answers.question: How do cash timings work?
answers.answer: Customers pay on 60-day terms, many late; we pay suppliers in 30 days; we carry about three months of timber stock

answers.question: What happened?
answers.answer: We hit the overdraft limit twice this quarter

answers.question: Which tools can the AI reach?
answers.answer: QuickBooks Online MCP read-only, bank statements as CSV

answers.question: What counts as success, and what must not break?
answers.answer: A cash buffer that never drops below $150,000 within six months. Cannot lose our two biggest retail customers

answers.question: Where does data live, who decides, what is unknown?
answers.answer: A Google Sheet. The owner decides with their accountant. Unknown: how late customers really pay on average

research.approach: Practitioners treat 'profitable but short of cash' as a timing problem, not a profit problem. They bridge profit to cash (what receivables, stock and payables absorbed), measure the cash conversion cycle as days of stock plus days of receivables minus days of payables, and measure real days-to-pay per customer from invoice and payment dates rather than trusting the terms. They then build a direct-method weekly forecast (receipts and payments by week from the ledgers, tied to the bank), run a bad case, roll it forward every week and compare it with the bank. Levers are ranked by cash freed, by when, and by what each costs; stretching suppliers and cutting stock are the ones that most often backfire, and key customers are handled with care, not pressure.

steps.name: Pull invoices, payments, bills, stock purchases and bank balances for the last 12 months
steps.why: Real payment dates and bank balances are the rawest material; the terms on paper are not.

steps.name: Tie the opening balance and open invoices and bills to the bank and the ledger
steps.why: A forecast from a wrong starting point is wrong every week.

steps.name: Measure real days to pay per customer and the cash conversion cycle
steps.why: Resolves the owner's stated unknown and shows which of stock, receivables or payables ties up the cash.

steps.name: Bridge profit to cash over the last year
steps.why: Shows where the 12% margin went before choosing levers.

steps.name: Build a weekly direct-method forecast with a base and a bad case
steps.why: Finds the first week below $150,000 and how bad it gets.

steps.name: Rank cash levers by cash freed, timing, cost and customer risk
steps.why: Collections, stock and supplier timing each free cash at a different speed and cost.

steps.name: Prepare careful customer and supplier steps for the owner to use
steps.why: Chasing and renegotiating are done by the owner; the two biggest customers need a relationship-first approach.

steps.name: Roll the forecast forward weekly and compare with the bank
steps.why: Catches a slide towards the floor weeks ahead.

pitfalls.text: Forecasting receipts on the 60-day terms instead of the days customers really take.
Partial and combined payments make days-to-pay look better or worse than it is.
Squeezing suppliers or cutting stock so hard that supply or a key customer's orders suffer.
A forecast built once and never compared with the bank, so errors compound.

plan.name: Keep cash above $150,000 for six months

capabilities.name: Read the ledger (QuickBooks Online MCP)
capabilities.why: Read invoices, payments, bills, stock purchases and the aging report. Read-only.

capabilities.name: Read bank statements (CSV)
capabilities.why: Actual balances and daily movements, the outside check on every forecast.

capabilities.name: Draft the Google Sheet
capabilities.why: Build the forecast and tracking tabs for the owner to open or import. Nothing is sent anywhere.

data.name: Customer invoices with due dates and payment dates, last 12 months
data.why: Measures how late each customer really pays.

QuickBooks Online: Reports, Invoices and Received Payments, export; plus A/R Aging Detail.

data.alternative: With only the aging report, days to pay is estimated from open invoices and marked low-confidence.

data.name: Supplier bills, due dates and timber purchases, last 12 months
data.why: Payments by week and the stock build-up.

routes.how: Read bills and bill payments with the QuickBooks Online MCP.
QuickBooks Online: A/P Aging Detail and Transaction List by Vendor, export.

data.why: Actual balances; ties the ledger to reality.

data.alternative: Without bank files the forecast opens on the ledger cash balance and is marked unverified.

routes.how: Read recurring bills and payroll journals from the ledger.

stages.name: Pin down the cash problem
stages.goal: Turn the request into a cash floor, a six-month window, the data we can reach and the limits around the two biggest customers. Writes BRIEF.md.

stages.name: Pull invoices, bills and bank balances
stages.goal: Pull 12 months of customer invoices and payments, supplier bills and bank statements into one working Google Sheet.

checks.name: Covers at least 12 months of invoices, payments, bills and bank movements
Invoice and bill totals by month equal the QuickBooks Online reports for the same dates within $1
Every bank account, including the overdraft, is present with no gaps in dates

stages.name: Check the starting numbers
stages.goal: Tie the opening cash balance, open invoices and open bills to the bank and the ledger, and find stale or unapplied items.

checks.name: Opening cash per bank statements equals the ledger cash balance within $1, or each reconciling item is listed
Open invoices by customer add up to the A/R aging total within $1
Invoices over 120 days old and unapplied payments are listed with their dollar total, and the share of open receivables is stated
Ends with CHECKED, LIMITED or UNRELIABLE and what that means for the forecast

stages.name: Find why profit does not turn into cash
stages.goal: Measure days to pay per customer, the cash conversion cycle and a profit-to-cash bridge for the last 12 months, and test the hypotheses.

checks.name: Payments are matched to invoices for at least 90% of paid-invoice dollars; partial and combined payments are flagged, not guessed
Average days to pay is weighted by invoice dollars and shown for each of the largest customers separately
Net profit plus change in receivables, stock, payables and other items equals the bank cash change within 2%, or the gap is named
Every listed hypothesis is SUPPORTED, REFUTED or UNKNOWN, with evidence
Each main finding names at least one competing explanation

stages.name: Forecast cash week by week
stages.goal: Build a direct-method weekly forecast for 26 weeks, using real days to pay, with a base case and a bad case, and mark the first week below $150,000.

checks.name: The opening balance equals the bank balance within $1
Receipts are timed from each customer's measured days to pay, with open invoices placed by due date plus that lag; confirmed and expected receipts are kept apart
The bad case delays each of the two biggest customers' payments by a further 15 days and states the lowest balance and the week it occurs
The first week below $150,000 in each case is stated, or 'none in 26 weeks'
Run on the prior 8 weeks, the forecast closing balances are within 10% of the bank's

stages.name: Rank the cash levers
stages.goal: Rank the levers (collections, timber stock, supplier timing, financing) by cash freed and when, cost, effect on the two biggest customers and confidence, and combine them into packages that hold $150,000.

checks.name: Each lever cites its finding and shows cash freed by week 4, 13 and 26, cost (discounts, interest, lost orders), effort and risk
Every lever says what it asks of the two biggest customers; any that touch them are marked for the owner only
Each package is rerun through the weekly forecast and shows whether the lowest balance stays at or above $150,000 in the bad case
Each package states its effect on net margin against last year's 12%

stages.name: Owner and accountant choose the package
stages.goal: The owner, with the accountant, picks the package and the order of actions. Record the reason if the top package is passed over.

checks.name: Chosen and passed-over packages are in decisions.jsonl
A reason is recorded wherever the top package was passed over

stages.name: Prepare the actions for the owner to use
stages.goal: For the chosen package, draft customer reminders by tier, a separate note for the two biggest customers, supplier talking points and a stock-ordering plan. The owner sends and decides; nothing goes out from here.

checks.name: Every action has an owner, a date and the cash it should free
Messages for the two biggest customers are separate, written for the relationship, and marked owner approves before use
Every amount and date in a draft matches the invoice list in the working sheet
Cash freed by the actions adds up to the chosen package within 5%

stages.optional_when: The chosen package contains no customer, supplier or stock actions.

stages.name: Roll the forecast forward each week
stages.goal: Each week, add the bank's actual balance, compare it with the forecast, update the first-breach week and flag a slide towards $150,000.

checks.name: The actual closing balance comes from the bank statement, not the ledger
Receipts and payments are compared with forecast by line; any line off by more than 10% and $10,000 is explained
A warning is raised when the forecast shows a week within $25,000 of the floor in the next 8 weeks
Each week uses the same definitions of confirmed and expected receipts

stages.name: Keep what we learned
stages.goal: Save rules (real days to pay per customer, stock cover, payment timing) with their scope and plan the next round.

checks.name: Each proposed rule says whether it holds for this job, this business or the playbook
States the lowest actual balance reached against $150,000 and whether the guardrails held

hypotheses.statement: Customers pay materially later than the 60-day terms.
hypotheses.test: Dollar-weighted days from due date to payment date for paid invoices in the last 12 months, plus age of open invoices.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Weighted average payment is 15 or more days after the due date.
hypotheses.refute_if: Weighted average is within 5 days of the due date.

hypotheses.statement: Most late money sits with a few customers, possibly the two biggest.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Five or fewer customers hold more than half of overdue dollars.
hypotheses.refute_if: Overdue dollars are spread across many customers with none above 15%.

hypotheses.statement: Timber stock is the biggest sink of cash.
hypotheses.test: Change in stock value over 12 months against change in receivables, and months of stock cover.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Stock grew by more than receivables did, or stock cover is above 3 months at the last three month-ends.
hypotheses.refute_if: Stock is flat and receivables grew more.

hypotheses.statement: The gap between paying suppliers in 30 days and being paid in 60+ days plus stock cover is the structural cause.
hypotheses.test: Days of stock plus days of receivables minus days of payables, at each of the last four quarter-ends.
hypotheses.confirm_if: The cycle is above 120 days and the overdraft hits follow the quarter-ends when it was longest.
hypotheses.refute_if: The cycle is under 90 days or the overdraft hits do not line up.

hypotheses.statement: Overdraft hits follow months of heavy timber purchasing.
hypotheses.test: Compare purchases in the month before each overdraft hit with the 12-month average.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Purchases before both hits exceeded 1.5 times the monthly average.
hypotheses.refute_if: Purchases were at or below average before the hits.

hypotheses.statement: Cash is leaving through items other than working capital (loan repayments, tax, owner drawings, equipment).
hypotheses.test: Bridge net profit to bank cash change and list the residual by item.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Non-working-capital outflows exceed 25% of net profit for the year.
hypotheses.refute_if: They are under 10% of net profit.

hypotheses.statement: The ledger overstates what is collectable because of old invoices or unapplied payments.
hypotheses.test: Receivables over 120 days and unapplied payments as a share of open receivables.
hypotheses.confirm_if: More than 5% of open receivables are over 120 days or unapplied.

measurement.window: Weekly for 26 weeks, comparing the forecast with the bank's closing balance.
measurement.min_volume: At least 4 weeks of actuals before judging the forecast's accuracy; a verdict on the floor needs all 26 weeks.
measurement.stop_rule: If the actual balance falls within $25,000 of the floor, stop the weekly cycle and bring the owner and accountant a revised plan.
